passage:
Dear Nikita,
Thank you for staying late on Friday. I keep thinking about the poster row. Someone in our group wanted to write that the registrar “doesn’t care about students.” I said no, and I checked the timetable myself. The library closes at eight because of the electricity contract, not laziness. So we changed the slogan to what is true: students need it open till eleven in exam weeks.
When Mr. Kulkarni from the office came to our stall, Tanvi hissed at him. I asked him to sit, poured him tea and showed him our numbers. He didn’t agree, but he took the petition to the meeting.
I’m not giving up on this. But if we lie about them, we lose our right to ask.
Hrithik

qa.q: Why does the library close at eight, according to Hrithik's letter?
qa.a: It closes at eight because of the electricity contract, not because of laziness.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel about the campaign after the poster row?
qa.a: Hrithik felt determined, saying he was not giving up, but he was firm that the campaign must stay truthful. He believed lying about the office would cost the group its right to ask.

qa.q: What choice made the meeting with Mr. Kulkarni useful?
qa.a: Hrithik invited him to sit, gave him tea and showed him the numbers instead of joining the hissing. Mr. Kulkarni still disagreed, but he took the petition to the meeting.

qa.q: How might Mr. Kulkarni have felt being hissed at and then given tea?
qa.a: He was probably startled and defensive at first, then a little disarmed by the courtesy. Taking the petition suggests he felt treated as a person rather than an enemy.

grounding: Shows a student volunteer staying firm on a cause while checking facts and treating the opposing office as human.

Samir, you asked how we kept it calm. Honestly, we didn’t always. I’m Kavitha, and our lane’s borewell was drying up, so forty of us went to the gate of the building site next door. Someone started shouting names at the site manager.
I stepped forward and said, “We’re here for the water, not against him.” Our placard claimed the site used ten times more than we did, and I asked who had checked. Nobody had. Rekha went to the municipal office the next morning, and the real figure was lower, though still large.
We reprinted the placard. Then the manager came out and listened for ten minutes. He said he would raise it. We hadn’t won, but people believed us after that.

qa.q: How many people went to the gate of the building site?
qa.a: Forty people went to the gate of the building site next door.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha step forward when someone started shouting names?
qa.a: Kavitha wanted the group to press its demand about the water without insulting the site manager. Kavitha's words, that they were there for the water, not against him, show a wish to keep the cause fair.

qa.q: What did the group do after finding the figure was wrong?
qa.a: They reprinted the placard with the correct, lower figure. That protected the group's credibility.

qa.q: How might the site manager have felt when the crowd stopped shouting and Kavitha spoke?
qa.a: He was probably wary at first, then more willing to listen, since he came out and listened for ten minutes. Being treated as a person rather than a target likely made that possible.

grounding: Shows a volunteer holding firm on a cause while treating an opponent as a person and correcting a wrong claim.
